definition.text: A model of oligopoly in which firms selling identical goods compete by setting prices, while buyers choose the quantities.

facts.text: Bertrand proposed it in 1883 as a reply to Cournot, arguing firms should undercut rivals' prices whenever those exceed marginal cost; Edgeworth formalised it in 1889.
It assumes identical goods, equal marginal costs, no capacity limits, simultaneous price setting and no search costs, so the lowest-priced firm takes the whole market.
The only equilibrium is price equal to marginal cost, with zero profit; it is a weak Nash equilibrium because deviating costs nothing.
Product differentiation, transport or search costs remove the result that price falls to marginal cost.
With capacity constraints (the Bertrand-Edgeworth model) a pure-strategy equilibrium may not exist, the Edgeworth paradox.

Bertrand industries are more competitive than Cournot ones because prices are strategic complements while quantities are strategic substitutes; Bertrand suits flexible capacity, Cournot suits output set in advance.
With network effects, firms may price aggressively to enlarge their customer base.

definition.text: The process of distinguishing a product from competitors' and from a firm's other products to make it more attractive to a target market.

facts.text: Edward Chamberlin proposed the concept in his 1933 book on monopolistic competition; it is inconsistent with perfect competition, which needs identical products.
Vertical differentiation rests on a characteristic consumers can rank objectively, such as quality; horizontal differentiation rests on subjective taste, such as colour; mixed combines both.
Sources of differentiation include quality, functional features or design, buyers' ignorance, advertising and availability in time and place; buyers must perceive the difference.
A green product may have lower environmental harm yet be inferior in other respects, so its appeal depends on advertising and social pressure.
A firm cannot charge a higher price if products are good substitutes; the further a product departs from others in its segment, the higher the price it can charge.
Low differentiation makes collusion harder to hold, since a small price cut can win a large share of the market.

title: Marginal revenue productivity theory of wages
article: Marginal revenue productivity theory of wages

definition.text: A neoclassical model in which wages equal the marginal revenue product of labour, the extra revenue an added unit of labour brings.

facts.text: A profit-maximising firm hires workers until marginal revenue product equals the wage; a worker whose marginal revenue is below the wage would cut profit.
Marginal revenue product is marginal product times marginal revenue, so hiring stops where MR times MP equals the wage, equivalent to MR equals MC.
In perfect competition MRP equals marginal physical product times price; a monopoly or imperfect competitor faces falling prices, so its MRP curve slopes down faster.
